To shorten something means to make it less long than it currently is. That's it at the heart. If something has a certain length — in space, in time, or in content — and you reduce that length, you have shortened it.
The Three Kinds of "Length" It Applies To

1. Physical length — the actual size of an object in space.

"She shortened the curtains because they were dragging on the floor."
"The tailor shortened the sleeves of his jacket."
"They shortened the rope so it wouldn't get tangled."

Here, something measurable and physical becomes smaller in its linear dimension.

2. Time / duration — how long something lasts.

"The doctor said smoking shortens your life."
"We shortened the meeting from two hours to forty-five minutes."
"Rain shortened the cricket match."

Here, the "length" isn't in space — it's in time. But the same logic applies: a span of time is made smaller.

3. Content / text — how much is said or written.

"Please shorten your essay — it's too long for the word limit."
"The editor shortened the article before publishing it."
"Can you shorten your speech? We only have ten minutes."

Here, the "length" is the amount of content. You remove some of it to make the whole thing shorter.

Transitive means you are acting on something — you are causing it to shorten.

"She shortened her hair."
"He shortened the deadline." (gave less time for completion)

Intransitive means something shortens on its own, without someone directly doing it.

"The days are shortening." (daylight hours are getting fewer as winter approaches)
"The gap between the two teams is shortening." (it is getting smaller on its own)

Both uses are correct. The difference is simply whether someone is acting on the thing, or the thing is changing by itself.
An Important Nuance: It Doesn't Tell You How Much

"Shorten" does not say how much shorter something becomes. It could be a little or a lot. If a 10-minute speech is cut to 9 minutes, it was shortened. If it's cut to 2 minutes, it was also shortened. The word only tells you that the length decreased — it doesn't quantify the reduction.

This is where precision matters, because several words are related but not identical.

Shorten vs. abbreviate
Abbreviate specifically means to shorten a word or a piece of text by using a reduced form. "Doctor" abbreviated becomes "Dr." You would not say "abbreviate a dress" or "abbreviate a meeting" — but you can say "shorten" in all of those situations. So "abbreviate" is narrower; "shorten" is broader.

Shorten vs. trim
Trim suggests removing a small amount from the edges — tidying up, neatening. It implies precision and a small degree of reduction. If you trim your hair, you remove a little bit. If you shorten your hair, you could remove any amount. "Trim" also carries the sense of neatness; "shorten" is simply about reducing length.

Shorten vs. cut
Cut is about the action of severing or slicing. You can cut something without shortening it (cut it in a direction that doesn't reduce its length). "Shorten" is about the result — the thing is now less long. You often cut something in order to shorten it, but they are different ideas.

Shorten vs. curtail
Curtail is more formal and usually means to stop something earlier than planned, or to limit it in scope. It often implies something that was intended to go on longer but was cut short. You curtail someone's rights, or a curtailed visit. "Shorten" is more neutral and general; "curtail" carries a sense of abrupt or reluctant stopping.

Shorten vs. abridge
Abridge applies almost exclusively to written or spoken works. An abridged novel is a shorter version that keeps the essential story but removes parts. It implies careful condensing with preservation of meaning. "Shorten" doesn't carry that careful preservation idea — you can shorten something poorly, cutting important parts. "Abridge" implies a considered editorial process.

Shorten vs. reduce
Reduce is very broad — you can reduce a price, reduce your stress, reduce a sauce (in cooking). "Reduce" applies to any kind of decrease. "Shorten" is specifically about length — physical, temporal, or textual. You would not say "shorten the price" or "shorten your anxiety."

This is worth being clear about, because learners sometimes confuse dimensions.

  • If something becomes less wide, you don't say "shorten" — you say "narrow."

    ✗ "Shorten the road." (doesn't mean make it narrower)
    ✓ "Narrow the road."

  • If something becomes less tall in a general sense (like a building), we typically say "lower" or "reduce the height," though for objects with a clear single linear dimension like a table leg or a post, "shorten" does work: "shorten the table leg."
  • If something becomes less heavy, you don't say "shorten" — you say "lighten" or "reduce the weight."
  • If something becomes less loud or intense, you don't say "shorten" — you say "lower," "reduce," or "soften."

Shorten is for length — not for weight, width, height in general, volume, or intensity.

"The odds shortened" — This comes from betting and probability. When people say "the odds shortened," they mean the probability of something happening is now considered higher, so the payout ratio has decreased. It's a figurative use: the range between the starting point and the expected outcome has become "shorter."

"Shorten someone's life" — A common and powerful use. It means a certain habit, event, or condition causes someone to die earlier than they otherwise would have. The length of a life is being reduced.

"Shorten the gap" — When two things (teams, countries, competitors) are separated by some measurable difference and that difference decreases, the gap has shortened. The distance between them — real or figurative — has become less.

"Shorten a name" — Informally, we shorten names. "Susannah" can be shortened to "Sue." "Gymnasium" is shortened to "gym." This is an informal way of saying "abbreviate" or "use a shorter form of."
A Quick Way to Check If "Shorten" Fits

Ask yourself: Is something becoming less long — in space, in time, or in amount of content?

If yes, "shorten" is likely the right word.

If you're talking about weight, width, intensity, or some other quality that isn't length, then "shorten" probably doesn't fit.

To shorten is to make something less long — whether that "length" is physical, measured in time, or measured in the amount of content — and the word says nothing about how much shorter, only that it has become shorter than it was.
